entries.0c668aa586f95bfced3c12798f53143dbcdb3ccd: <div sID="gen9862" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="26" osisID="Job.26" sID="Job.26"/> <div eID="gen9862" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9863" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen9864" type="x-p"/> This is Job's short reply to Bildad's short discourse, in which he is so far from contradicting him that he confirms what he had said, and out-does him in magnifying God and setting forth his power, to show what reason he had still to say, as he did (<reference osisRef="Job.13.2">ch. xiii. 2</reference>), "What you know, the same do I know also." I. He shows that Bildad's discourse was foreign to the matter he was discoursing of—though very true and good, yet not to the purpose, <reference osisRef="Job.26.2-Job.26.4">ver. 2-4</reference>. II. That it was needless to the person he was discoursing with; for he knew it, and believed it, and could speak of it as well as he and better, and could add to the proofs which he had produced of God's power and greatness, which he does in the rest of his discourse (<reference osisRef="Job.26.5-Job.26.15">ver. 5-13</reference>), concluding that, when they had both said what they could, all came short of the merit of the subject and it was still far from being exhausted, <reference osisRef="Job.26.14">ver. 14</reference>.
entries.ff47744c8d9588272ee3f89ce3ad20cac1785a4c: <div eID="gen9864" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen9863" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Job's Reproof of Bildad. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1520.)</title> <div sID="gen9865" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> But Job answered and said, <hi type="super">2</hi> How hast thou helped <hi type="italic">him that is</hi> without power? <hi type="italic">how</hi> savest thou the arm <hi type="italic">that hath</hi> no strength? <hi type="super">3</hi> How hast thou counselled <hi type="italic">him that hath</hi> no wisdom? and <hi type="italic">how</hi> hast thou plentifully declared the thing as it is? <hi type="super">4</hi> To whom hast thou uttered words? and whose spirit came from thee? <div eID="gen9865" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9866" type="x-p"/> One would not have thought that Job, when he was in so much pain and misery, could banter his friend as he does here and make himself merry with the impertinency of his discourse. Bildad thought that he had made a fine speech, that the matter was so weighty, and the language so fine, that he had gained the reputation both of an oracle and of an orator; but Job peevishly enough shows that his performance was not so valuable as he thought it and ridicules him for it. He shows, <div eID="gen9866" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9867" type="x-p"/> I. That there was no great matter to be found in it (<reference osisRef="Job.26.3">v. 3</reference>): <hi type="italic">How hast thou plentifully declared the thing as it is?</hi> This is spoken ironically, upbraiding Bildad with the good conceit he himself had of what he had said. 1. He thought he had spoken very clearly, had <hi type="italic">declared the thing as it is.</hi> He was very fond (as we are all apt to be) of his own notions, and thought they only were right, and true, and intelligible, and all other notions of the thing were false, mistaken, and confused; whereas, when we speak of the glory of God, we cannot declare the thing as it is, for we see it through a glass darkly, or but by reflection, and shall not see him as he is till we come to heaven. Here <hi type="italic">we cannot order our speech concerning him,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.37.19">ch. xxxvii. 19</reference>. 2. He thought he had spoken very fully, though in few words, that he had plentifully declared it, and, alas! it was but poorly and scantily that he declared it, in comparison with the vast compass and copiousness of the subject. <div eID="gen9867" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9868" type="x-p"/> II. That there was no great use to be made of it. <hi type="italic">Cui bono</hi>—<hi type="italic">What good hast thou done</hi> by all that thou hast said? <hi type="italic">How hast thou,</hi> with all this mighty flourish, <hi type="italic">helped him that is without power?</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.26.2">v. 2</reference>. <hi type="italic">How hast thou,</hi> with thy grave dictates, <hi type="italic">counselled</hi> him <hi type="italic">that has no wisdom?</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.26.3">v. 3</reference>. Job would convince him, 1. That he had done God no service by it, nor made him in the least beholden to him. It is indeed our duty, and will be our honour, to speak on God's behalf; but we must not think that he needs our service, or is indebted to us for it, nor will he accept it if it come from a spirit of contention and contradiction, and not from a sincere regard to God's glory. 2. That he had done his cause no service by it. He thought his friends were mightily beholden to him for helping them, at a dead lift, to make their part good against Job, when they were quite at a loss, and had no strength, no wisdom. Even weak disputants, when warm, are apt to think truth more beholden to them than it really is. 3. That he had done him no service by it. He pretended to convince, instruct, and comfort, Job; but, alas! what he had said was so little to the purpose that it would not avail to rectify any mistakes, nor to assist him either in bearing his afflictions or in getting good by them: "<hi type="italic">To whom has thou uttered words?</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.26.4">v. 4</reference>. Was it to me that thou didst direct thy discourse? And dost thou take me for such a child as to need these instructions? Or dost thou think them proper for one in my condition?" Every thing that is true and good is not suitable and seasonable. To one that was humbled, and broken, and grieved in spirit, as Job was, he ought to have preached of the grace and mercy of God, rather than of his greatness and majesty, to have laid before him the consolations rather than the terrors of the Almighty. Christ knows how to speak what is proper for the weary (<reference osisRef="Isa.50.4">Isa. l. 4</reference>), and his ministers should learn rightly to divide the word of truth, and not make those sad whom God would not have made sad, as Bildad did; and therefore Job asks him, <hi type="italic">Whose spirit came from thee?</hi> that is, "What troubled soul would ever be revived, and relieved, and brought to itself, by such discourses as these?" Thus are we often disappointed in our expectations from our friends who should comfort us, but the Comforter, who is the Holy Ghost, never mistakes in his operations nor misses of his end.
entries.88b85cd0cd2adbb693ef201172f65f654b952a2c: <div eID="gen9868" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Wisdom and Power of God. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1520.)</title> <div sID="gen9869" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">5</hi> Dead <hi type="italic">things</hi> are formed from under the waters, and the inhabitants thereof. <hi type="super">6</hi> Hell <hi type="italic">is</hi> naked before him, and destruction hath no covering. <hi type="super">7</hi> He stretcheth out the north over the empty place, <hi type="italic">and</hi> hangeth the earth upon nothing. <hi type="super">8</hi> He bindeth up the waters in his thick clouds; and the cloud is not rent under them. <hi type="super">9</hi> He holdeth back the face of his throne, <hi type="italic">and</hi> spreadeth his cloud upon it. <hi type="super">10</hi> He hath compassed the waters with bounds, until the day and night come to an end. <hi type="super">11</hi> The pillars of heaven tremble and are astonished at his reproof. <hi type="super">12</hi> He divideth the sea with his power, and by his understanding he smiteth through the proud. <hi type="super">13</hi> By his spirit he hath garnished the heavens; his hand hath formed the crooked serpent. <hi type="super">14</hi> Lo, these <hi type="italic">are</hi> parts of his ways: but how little a portion is heard of him? but the thunder of his power who can understand? <div eID="gen9869" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9870" type="x-p"/> The truth received a great deal of light from the dispute between Job and his friends concerning those points about which they differed; but now they are upon a subject in which they were all agreed, the infinite glory and power of God. How does truth triumph, and how brightly does it shine, when there appears no other strife between the contenders than which shall speak most highly and honourably of God and be most copious in showing forth his praise! It were well if all disputes about matters of religion might end thus, in <hi type="italic">glorifying God</hi> as Lord of all, and our Lord, <hi type="italic">with one mind and one mouth</hi> (<reference osisRef="Rom.15.6">Rom. xv. 6</reference>); for to that we have all attained, in that we are all agreed. <div eID="gen9870" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9871" type="x-p"/> I. Many illustrious instances are here given of the wisdom and power of God in the creation and preservation of the world. <div eID="gen9871" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9872" type="x-p"/> 1. If we look about us, to the earth and waters here below, we shall see striking instances of omnipotence, which we may gather out of these verses. (1.) <hi type="italic">He hangs the earth upon nothing,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.26.7">v. 7</reference>. The vast terraqueous globe neither rests upon any pillars nor hangs upon any axle-tree, and yet, by the almighty power of God, is firmly fixed in its place, poised with its own weight. The art of man could not hang a feather upon nothing, yet the divine wisdom hangs the whole earth so. It is <hi type="italic">ponderibus librata suis—poised by its own weight,</hi> so says the poet; it is <hi type="italic">upheld by the word of God's power,</hi> so says the apostle. What is hung upon nothing may serve us to set our feet on, and bear the weight of our bodies, but it will never serve us to set our hearts on, nor bear the weight of our souls. (2.) He <hi type="italic">sets bounds to the waters of the sea,</hi> and compasses them in (<reference osisRef="Job.26.10">v. 10</reference>), that they may not <hi type="italic">return to cover the earth;</hi> and these bounds shall continue unmoved, unshaken, unworn, <hi type="italic">till the day and night come to an end,</hi> when time shall be no more. Herein appears the dominion which Providence has over the raging waters of the sea, and so it is an instance of his power, <reference osisRef="Jer.5.22">Jer. v. 22</reference>. We see too the care which Providence takes of the poor sinful inhabitants of the earth, who, though obnoxious to his justice and lying at his mercy, are thus preserved from being overwhelmed, as they were once by the waters of a flood, and will continue to be so, because they are reserved unto fire. (3.) He <hi type="italic">forms dead things under the waters. Rephaim-giants, are formed under the waters,</hi> that is, vast creatures, of prodigious bulk, as whales, giant-like creatures, among the innumerable inhabitants of the water. So bishop Patrick. (4.) By mighty storms and tempests he shakes the mountains, which are here called <hi type="italic">the pillars of heaven</hi> (<reference osisRef="Job.26.11">v. 11</reference>), and even <hi type="italic">divides the sea, and smites through its proud waves,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.26.12">v. 12</reference>. At the presence of the Lord the <hi type="italic">sea flies</hi> and the <hi type="italic">mountains skip,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.114.3-Ps.114.4">Ps. cxiv. 3, 4</reference>. See <reference osisRef="Hab.3.6">Hab. iii. 6</reference>, &c. A storm furrows the waters, and does, as it were, divide them; and then a calm smites through the waves, and lays them flat again. See <reference osisRef="Ps.89.9-Ps.89.10">Ps. lxxxix. 9, 10</reference>. Those who think Job lived at, or after, the time of Moses, apply this to the dividing of the Red Sea before the children of Israel, and the drowning of the Egyptians in it. <hi type="italic">By his understanding he smiteth through Rahab;</hi> so the word is, and Rahab is often put for Egypt; as <reference osisRef="Ps.87.4">Ps. lxxxvii. 4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.51.9">Isa. li. 9</reference>. <div eID="gen9872" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9873" type="x-p"/> 2. If we consider hell beneath, though it is out of our sight, yet we may conceive the instances of God's power there. By <hi type="italic">hell and destruction</hi> (<reference osisRef="Job.26.6">v. 6</reference>) we may understand the grave, and those who are buried in it, that they are under the eye of God, though laid out of our sight, which may strengthen our belief of the resurrection of the dead. God knows where to find, and whence to fetch, all the scattered atoms of the consumed body. We may also consider them as referring to the place of the damned, where the separate souls of the wicked are in misery and torment. That is hell and destruction, which are said to be <hi type="italic">before the Lord</hi> (<reference osisRef="Prov.15.11">Prov. xv. 11</reference>), and here to be <hi type="italic">naked before him,</hi> to which it is probable there is an allusion, <reference osisRef="Rev.14.10">Rev. xiv. 10</reference>, where sinners are to be tormented <hi type="italic">in the presence of the holy angels</hi> (who attended the Shechinah) and <hi type="italic">in the presence of the Lamb.</hi> And this may give light to <reference osisRef="Job.26.5">v. 5</reference>, which some ancient versions read thus (and I think more agreeably to the signification of the word <hi type="italic">Rephaim): Behold, the giants groan under the waters, and those that dwell with them;</hi> and then follows, <hi type="italic">Hell is naked before him,</hi> typified by the drowning of the giants of the old world; so the learned Mr. Joseph Mede understands it, and with it illustrates <reference osisRef="Prov.21.16">Prov. xxi. 16</reference>, where hell is called <hi type="italic">the congregation of the dead;</hi> and it is the same word which is here used, and which he would there have rendered <hi type="italic">the congregation of the giants,</hi> in allusion to the drowning of the sinners of the old world. And is there any thing in which the majesty of God appears more dreadful than in the eternal ruin of the ungodly and the groans of the inhabitants of the land of darkness? Those that will not with angels fear and worship shall for ever with devils fear and tremble; and God therein will be glorified. <div eID="gen9873" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9874" type="x-p"/> 3. If we look up to heaven above, we shall see instances of God's sovereignty and power. (1.) <hi type="italic">He stretches out the north over the empty place,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.26.7">v. 7</reference>. So he did at first, when <hi type="italic">he stretched out the heavens like a curtain</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.104.2">Ps. civ. 2</reference>); and he still continues to keep them stretched out, and will do so till the general conflagration, when they shall be <hi type="italic">rolled together as a scroll,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.6.14">Rev. vi. 14</reference>. He mentions the north because his country (as ours) lay in the northern hemisphere; and the air is the empty place over which it is stretched out. See <reference osisRef="Ps.89.12">Ps. lxxxix. 12</reference>. What an empty place is this world in comparison with the other! (2.) He keeps the waters that are said to be <hi type="italic">above the firmament</hi> from pouring down upon the earth, as once they did (<reference osisRef="Job.26.8">v. 8</reference>): <hi type="italic">He binds up the waters in his thick clouds,</hi> as if they were tied closely in a bag, till there is occasion to use them; and, notwithstanding the vast weight of water so raised and laid up, yet <hi type="italic">the cloud is not rent under them,</hi> for then they would burst and pour out as a spout; but they do, as it were, distil through the cloud, and so come drop by drop, in mercy to the earth, in small rain, or great rain, as he pleases. (3.) He conceals the glory of the upper world, the dazzling lustre of which we poor mortals could not bear (<reference osisRef="Job.26.9">v. 9</reference>): <hi type="italic">He holds back the face of his throne,</hi> that light in which he dwells, <hi type="italic">and spreads a cloud upon it,</hi> through which <hi type="italic">he judges,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.22.13">ch. xxii. 13</reference>. God will have us to live by faith, not by sense; for this is agreeable to a state of probation. It were not a fair trial if the face of God's throne were visible now as it will be in the great day. <div eID="gen9874" type="x-p"/> <lg sID="gen9875"/> <l level="1" sID="gen9876"/>Lest his high throne, above expression bright,<l eID="gen9876" level="1"/> <l level="1" sID="gen9877"/>With deadly glory should oppress our sight,<l eID="gen9877" level="1"/> <l level="1" sID="gen9878"/>To break the dazzling force he draws a screen<l eID="gen9878" level="1"/> <l level="1" sID="gen9879"/>Of sable shades, and spreads his clouds between. Sir <hi type="small-caps">R. Blackmore</hi> .<l eID="gen9879" level="1"/> <lg eID="gen9875"/> <div sID="gen9880" type="x-p"/> (4.) The bright ornaments of heaven are the work of his hands (<reference osisRef="Job.26.13">v. 13</reference>): <hi type="italic">By his Spirit,</hi> the eternal Spirit that moved upon the face of the waters, <hi type="italic">the breath of his mouth</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.33.6">Ps. xxxiii. 6</reference>), <hi type="italic">he has garnished the heavens,</hi> not only made them, but beautified them, has curiously bespangled them with stars by night and painted them with the light of the sun by day. God, having made man to look upward (<hi type="italic">Os homini sublime dedit</hi>—<hi type="italic">To man he gave an erect countenance</hi>), has <hi type="italic">therefore</hi> garnished the heavens, to invite him to look upward, that, by pleasing his eye with the dazzling light of the sun and the sparkling light of the stars, their number, order, and various magnitudes, which, as so many golden studs, beautify the canopy drawn over our heads, he may be led to admire the great Creator, the Father and fountain of lights, and to say, "If the pavement be so richly inlaid, what must the palace be! If the visible heavens be so glorious, what are those that are out of sight!" From the beauteous garniture of the ante-chamber we may infer the precious furniture of the presence-chamber. If stars be so bright, what are angels! What is meant here by <hi type="italic">the crooked serpent</hi> which his hands have formed is not certain. Some make it part of the garnishing of the heavens, the milky-way, say some; some particular constellation, so called, say others. It is the same word that is used for leviathan (<reference osisRef="Isa.27.1">Isa. xxvii. 1</reference>), and probably may be meant of the whale or crocodile, in which appears much of the power of the Creator; and why may not Job conclude with that inference, when God himself does so? <reference osisRef="Job.41.1-Job.41.34">ch. xli.</reference> <div eID="gen9880" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9881" type="x-p"/> II. He concludes, at last, with an awful <hi type="italic">et cætera</hi> (<reference osisRef="Job.26.14">v. 14</reference>): <hi type="italic">Lo, these are parts of his ways,</hi> the out-goings of his wisdom and power, the ways in which he walks and by which he makes himself known to the children of men. Here, 1. He acknowledges, with adoration, the discoveries that were made of God. These things which he himself had said, and which Bildad had said, are his ways, and this is heard of him; this is something of God. But, 2. He admires the depth of that which is undiscovered. This that we have said is but part of his ways, a small part. What we know of God is nothing in comparison with what is in God and what God is. After all the discoveries which God has made to us, and all the enquiries we have made after God, still we are much in the dark concerning him, and must conclude, <hi type="italic">Lo, these are but parts of his ways.</hi> Something we hear of him by his works and by his word; but, alas! <hi type="italic">how little a portion is heard of him?</hi> heard by us, heard from us! We know but in part; we prophesy but in part. When we have said all we can, concerning God, we must even do as St. Paul does (<reference osisRef="Rom.11.33">Rom. xi. 33</reference>); despairing to find the bottom, we must sit down at the brink, and adore the depth: <hi type="italic">O the depth of the wisdom and knowledge of God!</hi> It is but a little portion that we hear and know of God in our present state. He is infinite and incomprehensible; our understandings and capacities are weak and shallow, and the full discoveries of the divine glory are reserved for the future state. Even <hi type="italic">the thunder of his power</hi> (that is, his powerful thunder), one of the lowest of his ways here in our own region, we cannot understand. See <reference osisRef="Job.37.4-Job.37.5">ch. xxxvii. 4, 5</reference>. Much less can we understand the utmost force and extent of his power, the terrible efforts and operations of it, and particularly <hi type="italic">the power of his anger,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.90.11">Ps. xc. 11</reference>. God is great, and we know him not.  <chapter eID="Job.26"/> <div eID="gen9881" type="x-p"/>

entries.84b918d0081da95c1403743416c5335fbda4d10b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5005"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 26</title> <div sID="gen7404" type="x-p"/> THIRD SERIES.<div eID="gen7404" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Job.26.1-Job.26.14">Job 26:1-14</reference>. Job's Reply.</title> <div sID="gen7405" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5005"/><hi type="bold">2-3. without power ... no strength ... no wisdom--</hi>The negatives are used instead of the positives, powerlessness, &c., designedly (so <reference osisRef="Isa.31.8">Is 31:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.32.21">De 32:21</reference>). Granting I am, as you say (<reference osisRef="Job.18.17">Job 18:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.15.2">15:2</reference>), powerlessness itself, &c. "How hast thou helped such a one?"<div eID="gen7405" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7406" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">savest--</hi>supportest. <div eID="gen7406" type="x-p"/>
entries.ff1e668c53133610824ce37e7bcc69b47d40d0a8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5007"/><div sID="gen7408" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5007"/>4. For whose instruction were thy words meant? If for me I know the subject (God's omnipotence) better than my instructor; <reference osisRef="Job.26.5-Job.26.14">Job 26:5-14</reference> is a sample of Job's knowledge of it.<div eID="gen7408" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7409" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">whose spirit--</hi>not that of God (<reference osisRef="Job.32.8">Job 32:8</reference>); nay, rather, the borrowed sentiment of Eliphaz (Job 4:17-19; 15:<reference osisRef="Job.19.14-Job.19.16">14-16</reference>). <div eID="gen7409" type="x-p"/>
entries.ac3971a56617bdf558dddb9750e2b13ca0fdd624: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5008"/><div sID="gen7410" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5008"/>5-14. As before in the ninth and twelfth chapters, Job had shown himself not inferior to the friends' inability to describe God's greatness, so now he describes it as manifested in hell (the world of the dead), <reference osisRef="Job.26.5">Job 26:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.26.6">6</reference>; on earth, <reference osisRef="Job.26.7">Job 26:7</reference>; in the sky, <reference osisRef="Job.26.8-Job.26.11">Job 26:8-11</reference>; the sea, <reference osisRef="Job.26.12">Job 26:12</reference>; the heavens, <reference osisRef="Job.26.13">Job 26:13</reference>.<div eID="gen7410" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7411" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Dead things are formed--</hi>Rather, "The souls of the dead (Rephaim) tremble." Not only does God's power exist, as Bildad says (<reference osisRef="Job.25.2">Job 25:2</reference>), "in high places" (heaven), but reaches to the region of the dead. Rephaim here, and in <reference osisRef="Prov.21.16">Pr 21:16</reference> and <reference osisRef="Isa.14.9">Is 14:9</reference>, is from a Hebrew root, meaning "to be weak," hence "deceased"; in <reference osisRef="Gen.14.5">Ge 14:5</reference> it is applied to the Canaanite giants; perhaps in derision, to express their weakness, in spite of their gigantic size, as compared with Jehovah [Umbreit]; or, as the imagination of the living magnifies apparitions, the term originally was applied to ghosts, and then to giants in general [Magee].<div eID="gen7411" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7412" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">from under--</hi>Umbreit joins this with the previous word "tremble from beneath" (so <reference osisRef="Isa.14.9">Is 14:9</reference>). But the Masoretic text joins it to "under the waters." Thus the place of the dead will be represented as "under the waters" (<reference osisRef="Ps.18.4">Psa 18:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.18.5">5</reference>); and the waters as under the earth (<reference osisRef="Ps.24.2">Psa 24:2</reference>). Magee well translates thus: "The souls of the dead tremble; (the places) under the waters, and their inhabitants." Thus the Masoretic connection is retained; and at the same time the parallel clauses are evenly balanced. "The inhabitants of the places under the waters" are those in Gehenna, the lower of the two parts into which Sheol, according to the Jews, is divided; they answer to "destruction," that is, the place of the wicked in <reference osisRef="Job.26.6">Job 26:6</reference>, as "Rephaim" (<reference osisRef="Job.26.5">Job 26:5</reference>) to "Hell" (Sheol) (<reference osisRef="Job.26.6">Job 26:6</reference>). "Sheol" comes from a Hebrew root--"ask," because it is insatiable (<reference osisRef="Prov.27.20">Pr 27:20</reference>); or "ask as a loan to be returned," implying Sheol is but a temporary abode, previous to the resurrection; so for English Version "formed," the Septuagint and Chaldee translate; shall be born, or born again, implying the dead are to be given back from Sheol and born again into a new state [Magee]. <div eID="gen7412" type="x-p"/>

entries.bb0830565acf587a7071463362e98a34478b089c: <div eID="gen17100" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen17101" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen17102" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen17102" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen17101" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen17103" type="x-p"/> Job, perceiving that his friends could no longer support their arguments on the ground they had assumed, sharply reproves them for their want both of wisdom and feeling, <reference osisRef="Job.26.1-Job.26.4">Job 26:1-4</reference>; shows that the power and wisdom of God are manifest in the works of creation and providence; gives several proofs; and then adds that these are a small specimen of his infinite skill and unlimited power, <reference osisRef="Job.26.5-Job.26.14">Job 26:5-14</reference>.
entries.0d24ce485b29320183ccd46b0bb5e325d49e91fa: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen17103" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17104" type="x-p"/> How hast thou helped him - This seems a species of irony. How wonderfully hast thou counselled the unskilful and strengthened the weak! Alas for you! ye could not give what ye did not possess! In this way the Chaldee understood these verses: "Why hast thou pretended to give succor, when thou art without strength? And save, while thy arm is weak? Why hast thou given counsel, when thou art without understanding? And supposest that thou hast shown the very essence of wisdom?"
entries.93761bc1c935b5029289ef282712dfad8e4d2331: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen17104" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17105" type="x-p"/> Whose spirit came from thee? - Mr. Good renders the verse thus: From whom hast thou pillaged speeches? And whose spirit hath issued forth from thee? The retort is peculiarly severe; and refers immediately to the proverbial sayings which in several of the preceding answers have been adduced against the irritated sufferer; for which see <reference osisRef="Job.8.11-Job.8.19">Job 8:11-19</reference>; 15:20-35, some of which he has already complained of, as in <reference osisRef="Job.12.3">Job 12:3</reference>, and following. I concur most fully therefore with Dr. Stock in regarding the remainder of this chapter as a sample, ironically exhibited by Job, of the harangues on the power and greatness of God which he supposes his friends to have taken out of the mouths of other men, to deck their speeches with borrowed lustre. Only, in descanting on the same subject, he shows how much he himself can go beyond them in eloquence and sublimity. <div eID="gen17105" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17106" type="x-p"/> Job intimates that, whatever spirit they had, it was not the Spirit of God, because in their answers falsehood was found.
entries.b448a6d1de40a491239a912afbc2ddc52c78a969: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen17106" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17107" type="x-p"/> Dead things are formed from under the waters - This verse, as it stands in our version, seems to convey no meaning; and the Hebrew is obscure; הרפאים, harephaim, "the Rephaim," certainly means not dead things; nor can there be any propriety in saying that dead things, or things without life, are formed under the waters, for such things are formed everywhere in the earth, and under the earth, as well as under the waters. <div eID="gen17107" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17108" type="x-p"/> The Vulgate translates: Ecce gigantes gemunt sub aquis, et qui habitant cum eis. "Behold the giants, and those who dwell with them, groan from under the waters." <div eID="gen17108" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17109" type="x-p"/> The Septuagint: Μη γιγαντες μαιωθησονται ὑποκατωθεν ὑδατος, και των γειτονων αυτου; "Are not the giants formed from under the waters, and their neighbors?" <div eID="gen17109" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17110" type="x-p"/> The Chaldee: אפשר דגבריא דמתמזמזין יתברין ואנון מלרע למיא ומשריתהון eposhar degibraiya demithmazmezin yithbareyan veinnun millera lemaiya umashreiyatehon, "Can the trembling giants be regenerated, when they and their hosts are under the water?" <div eID="gen17110" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17111" type="x-p"/> The Syriac and Arabic: "Behold, the giants are slain, and are drawn out of the water." None of these appear to give any sense by which the true meaning can be determined. <div eID="gen17111" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17112" type="x-p"/> There is probably here an allusion to the destruction of the earth by the general deluge. Moses, speaking concerning the state of the earth before the flood, says, <reference osisRef="Gen.6.4">Gen 6:4</reference>, "There were giants נפלים nephilim, in the earth in those days." Now it is likely that Job means the same by רפאים rephaim as Moses does by the nephilim; and that both refer to the antediluvians, who were all, for their exceeding great iniquities, overwhelmed by the waters of the deluge. Can those mighty men and their neighbors, all the sinners who have been gathered to them since, be rejected from under the waters, by which they were judicially overwhelmed? <div eID="gen17112" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17113" type="x-p"/> Mr. Good thinks the shades of the heroes of former times, the gigantic spectres, the mighty or enormous dead, are meant. <div eID="gen17113" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17114" type="x-p"/> I greatly question whether sea-monsters be not intended, such as porpoises, sharks, narwals, grampuses, and whales. We know, however that an opinion anciently prevailed, that the Titans, a race of men of enormous stature, rebelled against the gods, and endeavored to scale heaven by placing one mountain on the top of another; and that they and their structure were cast down by the thunder of the deities, and buried under the earth and sea; and that their struggles to arise produce the earthquakes which occur in certain countries. Now although this opinion is supported by the most respectable antiquity among the heathens, it is not to be supposed that in the word of God there can be any countenance given to an opinion at once as absurd as it is monstrous. (But still the poet may use the language of the common people). I must therefore either refer the passage here to the antediluvians, or to the vast sea-monsters mentioned above.
entries.8190df9ee0054628836a70b46ddcc75ccbf6eb5e: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen17114" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17115" type="x-p"/> Hell is naked before him - Sheol, the place of the dead, or of separate spirits, is always in his view. And there is no covering to Abaddon - the place of the destroyer, where destruction reigns, and where those dwell who are eternally separated from God. The ancients thought that hell or Tartarus was a vast space in the center, or at the very bottom of the earth. So Virgil, Aen. lib. vi., ver. 577: - - Tum Tartarus ipse <div eID="gen17115" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17116" type="x-p"/> Bis patet in praeceps tantum, tenditque sub umbras, <div eID="gen17116" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17117" type="x-p"/> Quantus ad aethereum coeli suspectus Olympum <div eID="gen17117" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17118" type="x-p"/> Hic genus antiquum terrae, Titania pubes, <div eID="gen17118" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17119" type="x-p"/> Fulmine dejecti, fundo volvuntur in imo. "Full twice as deep the dungeon of the fiends, <div eID="gen17119" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17120" type="x-p"/> The huge Tartarean gloomy gulf, descends <div eID="gen17120" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17121" type="x-p"/> Below these regions, as these regions lie <div eID="gen17121" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17122" type="x-p"/> From the bright realms of yon ethereal sky. <div eID="gen17122" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17123" type="x-p"/> Here roar the Titan race, th' enormous birth; <div eID="gen17123" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17124" type="x-p"/> The ancient offspring of the teeming earth. <div eID="gen17124" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17125" type="x-p"/> Pierced by the burning bolts of old they fell, <div eID="gen17125" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17126" type="x-p"/> And still roll bellowing in the depths of hell." <div eID="gen17126" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17127" type="x-p"/> Pitt. <div eID="gen17127" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17128" type="x-p"/> And some have supposed that there is an allusion to this opinion in the above passage, as well as in several others in the Old Testament; but it is not likely that the sacred writers would countenance an opinion that certainly has nothing in fact or philosophy to support it. Yet still a poet may avail himself of popular opinions.
entries.ed357362b97b74f8727fe6b569651e7eeca95cee: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen17128" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17129" type="x-p"/> He stretcheth out the north over the empty place - על תהו al tohu, to the hollow waste. The same word as is used, <reference osisRef="Gen.1.2">Gen 1:2</reference>, The earth was without form, תהו tohu. The north must here mean the north pole, or northern hemisphere; and perhaps what is here stated may refer to the opinion that the earth was a vast extended plain, and the heavens poised upon it, resting on this plain all round the horizon. Of the south the inhabitants of Idumea knew nothing; nor could they have any notion of inhabitants in that hemisphere. <div eID="gen17129" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17130" type="x-p"/> Hangeth the earth upon nothing - The Chaldee says: "He lays the earth upon the waters, nothing sustaining it."
entries.c003738365d1bd5ad6c76759bd77f4bba091424c: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen17130" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17131" type="x-p"/> He bindeth up the waters - Drives the aqueous particles together, which were raised by evaporation, so that, being condensed, they form clouds which float in the atmosphere, till, meeting with strong currents of wind, or by the agency of the electric fluid, they are farther condensed; and then, becoming too heavy to be sustained in the air, fall down in the form of rain, when, in this poetic language, the cloud is rent under them.
entries.e79fe24f6cbe890246241fe41d072cd4756d7175: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen17131" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17132" type="x-p"/> He holdeth back the face of his throne - Though all these are most elegant effects of an omniscient and almighty power, yet the great Agent is not personally discoverable; he dwelleth in light unapproachable, and in mercy hides himself from the view of his creatures. The words, however may refer to those obscurations of the face of heaven, and the hiding of the body of the sun, when the atmosphere is laden with dense vapours, and the rain begins to be poured down on the earth.
entries.faf9987566373dd8d4d2237fa8c26687c061155a: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen17132" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17133" type="x-p"/> He hath compassed the waters with bounds - Perhaps this refers merely to the circle of the horizon, the line that terminates light and commences darkness, called here עד תכלית אור עם חשך ad tachlith or im chosech, "until the completion of light with darkness." Or, if we take תכלית tachlith here to be the same with תכלת techeleth, <reference osisRef="Exo.25.4">Exo 25:4</reference>, and elsewhere, which we translate blue, it may mean that sombre sky-blue appearance of the horizon at the time of twilight, i.e., between light and darkness; the line where the one is terminating and the other commencing. Or, He so circumscribes the waters, retaining them in their own place, that they shall not be able to overflow the earth until day and night, that is, time itself, come to an end.
entries.ec88309c85fc8fa01d615f697a934a4df7e8b992: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen17133" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17134" type="x-p"/> The pillars of heaven tremble - This is probably a poetical description either of thunder, or of an earthquake: - "He shakes creation with his nod; <div eID="gen17134" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17135" type="x-p"/> Earth, sea, and heaven, confess him God." <div eID="gen17135" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17136" type="x-p"/> But there may be an allusion to the high mountains, which were anciently esteemed by the common people as the pillars on which the heavens rested; and when these were shaken with earthquakes, it might be said the pillars of heaven tremble. Mount Atlas was supposed to be one of those pillars, and this gave rise to the fable of Atlas being a man who bore the heavens on his shoulders. The Greek and Roman poets frequently use this image. Thus Silius Italicus, lib. i., ver. 202: - <div eID="gen17136" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17137" type="x-p"/> Atlas subducto tracturus vertice coelum: <div eID="gen17137" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17138" type="x-p"/> Sidera nubiferum fulcit caput, aethereasque <div eID="gen17138" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17139" type="x-p"/> Erigit aeternum compages ardua cervix: <div eID="gen17139" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17140" type="x-p"/> Canet barba gelu, frontemque immanibus umbris <div eID="gen17140" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17141" type="x-p"/> Pinea silva premit; vastant cava tempora venti <div eID="gen17141" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17142" type="x-p"/> Nimbosoque ruunt spumantia flumina rictu. "Atlas' broad shoulders prop th' incumbent skies: <div eID="gen17142" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17143" type="x-p"/> Around his cloud-girt head the stars arise. <div eID="gen17143" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17144" type="x-p"/> His towering neck supports th' ethereal way; <div eID="gen17144" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17145" type="x-p"/> And o'er his brow black woods their gloom display. <div eID="gen17145" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17146" type="x-p"/> Hoar is his beard; winds round his temples roar; <div eID="gen17146" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17147" type="x-p"/> And from his jaws the rushing torrents pour." <div eID="gen17147" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17148" type="x-p"/> J. B. C.
entries.062facbeab4e473244abb5749e6e03f65c487043: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen17148" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17149" type="x-p"/> He divideth the sea with his power - Here is a manifest allusion to the passage of the Red Sea by the Israelites, and the overthrow of Pharaoh and his host, according to the opinion of the most eminent critics. <div eID="gen17149" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17150" type="x-p"/> He smiteth through the proud - רהב Rahab, the very name by which Egypt is called <reference osisRef="Isa.51.9">Isa 51:9</reference>, and elsewhere. Calmet remarks: "This appears to refer only to the passage of the Red Sea, and the destruction of Pharaoh. Were we not prepossessed with the opinion that Job died before Moses, every person at the first view of the subject must consider it in this light." I am not thus prepossessed. Let Job live when he might, I am satisfied the Book of Job was written long after the death of Moses, and not earlier than the days of Solomon, if not later. The farther I go in the work, the more this conviction is deepened; and the opposite sentiment appears to be perfectly gratuitous.
entries.2b98d60dbd21d847b353f3de3a34a8eb4eb99124: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen17150" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17151" type="x-p"/> By his Spirit he hath garnished the heavens - See the observations below.
entries.c69682aff28ac9f65b912ce32bc3d793be2666c7: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen17151" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17152" type="x-p"/> Lo, these are parts of his ways - קצות ketsoth, the ends or extremities, the outlines, an indistinct sketch, of his eternal power and Godhead. <div eID="gen17152" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17153" type="x-p"/> How little a portion is heard - שמץ shemets, a mere whisper; admirably opposed, as Mr. Good has well observed, to רעם raam, the thunder, mentioned in the next clause. As the thunder is to a whisper, so are the tremendous and infinitely varied works of God to the faint outlines exhibited in the above discourse. Every reader will relish the dignity, propriety, and sense of these expressions. They force themselves on the observation of even the most heedless. By his Spirit he hath garnished the heavens - Numerous are the opinions relative to the true meaning of this verse. Some think it refers to the clearing of the sky after a storm, such as appears to be described <reference osisRef="Job.26.11">Job 26:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.26.12">Job 26:12</reference>; and suppose his Spirit means the wind, which he directs to sweep and cleanse the face of the sky, by which the splendor of the day or the lustre of the night is restored: and by the crooked, flying, or aerial serpent, as it is variously rendered, the ecliptic is supposed to be meant, as the sun's apparent course in it appears to be serpentine, in his approach to and recession from each of the tropics. This tortuous line may be seen on any terrestrial globe. Many will object to this notion as too refined for the time of Job; but this I could easily admit, as astronomy had a very early existence among the Arabians, if not its origin. But with me the chief objection lies against the obscurity of the allusion, if it be one; for it must require no small ingenuity, and almost the spirit of divination, to find out the sun's oblique path in the zodiac in the words His hand hath formed the crooked serpent. Others have imagined that the allusion is to the lightning in that zigzag form which it assumes when discharged from one cloud into another during a thunder storm. This is at once a natural and very apparent sense. To conduct and manage the lightning is most certainly a work which requires the skill and omnipotence of God, as much as garnishing the heavens by his Spirit, dividing the sea by his power, or causing the pillars of heaven to tremble by his reproof. Others think that the act of the creation of the solar system is intended to be expressed, which is in several parts of the sacred writings attributed to the Spirit of God; (<reference osisRef="Gen.1.2">Gen 1:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Psa.33.6">Psa 33:6</reference>); and that the crooked serpent means either Satan, who deceived our first parents, or huge aquatic animals; for in <reference osisRef="Isa.27.1">Isa 27:1</reference>, we find the leviathan and dragon of the sea called נחש ברח nachash bariach, the very terms that are used by Job in this place: "In that day the Lord with his sore and great and strong sword shall punish leviathan, the piercing serpent, (נחש ברח nachash bariach), even leviathan, that crooked serpent, (נחש עקלתון nachash akallathon), and he shall slay the dragon (התנין hattannin) that is in the sea." And we know that in <reference osisRef="Gen.1.21">Gen 1:21</reference> התנינם הגדלים hattanninim haggedolim, which we translate great whales, includes all sea-monsters or vast aquatic animals. Calmet, who without hesitation adopts this sentiment, says: "I see no necessity to have recourse to allegory here. After having exhibited the effects of the sovereign power of God in the heavens, in the clouds, in the vast collection of waters in the sea, it was natural enough for Job to speak of the production of fishes." The intelligent Dr. Sherlock gives another interpretation. After strongly expressing his disapprobation of the opinion that Job should descend, after speaking of the creation of the heavens and their host, to the formation of snakes and adders, he supposes "that Job here intended to oppose that grand religious system of sabaeism which prevailed in his time, and to which, in other parts of this book, he alludes; a system which acknowledged two opposite independent principles by which the universe was governed, and paid Divine adoration to the celestial luminaries. Suppose, therefore, Job to be acquainted with the fall of man, and the part ascribed to the serpent of the introduction of evil, see how aptly the parts cohere. In opposition to the idolatrous practice of the time, he asserts God to be the maker of all the host of heaven: By his Spirit he garnished the heavens. In opposition to the false notion of two independent principles, he asserts God to be the maker of him who was the author of evil: His hand hath formed the crooked serpent. You see how properly the garnishing of the heavens and the forming of the serpent are joined together. That this is the ancient traditionary explication of this place, we have undeniable evidence from the translation of the Septuagint, who render the latter part of this verse, which relates to the serpent, in this manner: Προσταγματι δε εθανατωσε δρακοντα αποστατην, By a decree he destroyed the apostate dragon. The Syriac and Arabic versions are to the same effect: And his hand slew the flying serpent. "These translators apply the place to the punishment inflicted on the serpent; and it comes to the same thing, for the punishing the serpent is as clear an evidence of God's power over the author of evil as the creating him. We need not wonder to see so much concern in this book to maintain the supremacy of God, and to guard it against every false notion; for this was the theme, the business of the author." - Bp. Sherlock on Prophecy, Diss. ii. <div eID="gen17153" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17154" type="x-p"/> From the contradictory opinions on this passage, the reader will no doubt feel cautious what mode of interpretation he adopts, and the absolute necessity of admitting no texts of doubtful interpretation as vouchers for the essential doctrines of Christianity. Neither metaphors, allegories, similes, nor figurative expressions of any kind, should ever be adduced or appealed to as proofs of any article in the Christian faith. We have reason to be thankful that this is at present the general opinion of the most rational divines of all sects and parties, and that the allegory and metaphor men are everywhere vanishing from the meridian and sinking under the horizon of the Church. Scriptural Christianity is prevailing with a strong hand, and going forward with a firm and steady step.  <chapter eID="Job.26"/> <div eID="gen17154" type="x-p"/>

entries.d87ffb9029f98687e10647953eeedfc2505be7d0: <reference osisRef="Job.26.1-Job.4.1">Job 26:1-4  1</reference>  Then Job began, and said:  2  How has thou helped him that is without power, <div eID="gen7977" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7978" type="x-p"/> Raised the arm that hath no strength!   3  How hast thou counselled him that hath no wisdom, <div eID="gen7978" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7979" type="x-p"/> And fully declared the essence of the matter!   4  To whom hast thou uttered words, <div eID="gen7979" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7980" type="x-p"/> And whose breath proceeded from thee? <div eID="gen7980" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7981" type="x-p"/> Bildad is the person addressed, and the exclamations in <reference osisRef="Job.26.2">Job 26:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.26.3">Job 26:3</reference> are ironical: how thy speech contains nothing whatever that might help me, the supposedly feeble one, in conquering my affliction and my temptation; me, the supposedly ignorant one, in comprehending man’s mysterious lot, and mine! ללא־כח, according to the idea, is only equivalent to כח לו (אין) לאשׁר לא, and זרוע לא־עז equivalent to זרוע בלא־עז (לא עז לו); the former is the <hi type="italic">abstr. pro concreto,</hi> the latter the genitival connection - the arm of the no-power, i.e., powerless (Ges. §152, 1). The powerless one is Job himself, not God (Merc., Schlottm.), as even the choice of the verbs, <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.26.2">Job 26:2</reference></hi>, <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.26.3">Job 26:3</reference></hi>, shows. Respecting תּוּשׁיּה, which we have translated essentiality, duration, completion, we said, on <reference osisRef="Job.5.12">Job 5:12</reference>, that it is formed from ישׁ (vid., <reference osisRef="Prov.8.21">Pro 8:21</reference>), not directly indeed, but by means of a verb ושׁי brev a fo  (ושׁה), in the signification subsistere (comp. Arab. <hi type="italic">kân</hi>, and Syriac קום);<note placement="foot">Comp. also Spiegel, <hi type="italic">Grammatik der Huzväresch-Sprache,</hi> S. 103.</note> it is a <hi type="italic">Hophal</hi>-formation (like תּוּגה), and signifies, so to speak, durability, <hi type="italic">subsistentia, substantia,</hi> ὑπόστασις, so that the comparison of ושׁי with אשׁשׁ, Arab. <hi type="italic">'ss</hi> (whence אשׁישׁ, Arab. <hi type="italic">ası̂s , asâs ,</hi> etc., <hi type="italic">fundamentum</hi>) is forced upon one, and the relationship to the Sanskrit <hi type="italic">as</hi> (<hi type="italic">asmi</hi> = εἰμὶ) can remain undecided. The observation of J. D. Michaelis<note placement="foot">Against the comparison of the Arab. <hi type="italic">wâsâ , solari,</hi> by Michaelis, Ges., and others (who assume the primary significations <hi type="italic">solatium, auxilium</hi>), Lagarde (<hi type="italic">Anmerkungen zur griech. Uebersetzung der Proverbien,</hi> 1863, S. 57f.) correctly remarks that Arab. <hi type="italic">wâsâ ,</hi> is only a change of letters of the common language for Arab. <hi type="italic">âsâ ;</hi> but Arab. <hi type="italic">wâšâ</hi>, to finish painting (whence Arab. <hi type="italic">twšyt</hi>, decoration), or ושׁה as a transposition from שׁוה, to be level, simple (Hitzig on <reference osisRef="Prov.3.21">Pro 3:21</reference>), leads to no suitable sense.</note> to the contrary, <hi type="italic">Supplem</hi>. p. 1167: <hi type="italic">non placent in linguis ejusmodi etyma metaphysica nimis a vulgari sensu remota; philosophi in scholis ejusmodi vocabula condunt, non plebs,</hi> is removed by the consideration that תושׁיה, which out of Prov. and Job occurs only in <reference osisRef="Isa.28.29">Isa 28:29</reference>, Mich. <reference osisRef="Job.6.9">Job 6:9</reference>, is a Chokma-word: it signifies here, as frequently, <hi type="italic">vera et realis sapientia</hi> (J. H. Michaelis). The speech of Bildad is a proof of poverty of thought, of which he himself gives the evidence. His words - such is the thought of <reference osisRef="Job.26.4">Job 26:4</reference> - are altogether inappropriate, inasmuch as they have no reference whatever to the chief point of Job’s speech; and they are, moreover, not his own, but the suggestion of another, and that not God, but Eliphaz, from whom Bildad has borrowed the substance of his brief declamation. Since this is the meaning of <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.26.4">Job 26:4</reference></hi>, it might seem as though את־מי were intended to signify by whose assistance (Arnh., Hahn); but as the poet also, in <reference osisRef="Job.31.37">Job 31:37</reference>, comp. <reference osisRef="Ezek.43.10">Eze 43:10</reference>, uses הגּיד <hi type="italic">seq. acc.,</hi> in the sense of explaining anything to any one, to instruct him concerning anything, it is to be interpreted: to whom hast thou divulged the words (lxx, τίνι ἀνήγγειλας ῥήματα), i.e., thinking and designing thereby to affect him? <div eID="gen7981" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7982" type="x-p"/> In what follows, Job now continues the description of God’s exalted rule, which Bildad had attempted, by tracing it through every department of creation; and thus proves by fact, that he is wanting neither in a recognition nor reverence of God the almighty Ruler.
entries.b8e905b9c0a040fd12a8b1657c0c8214bfc5d9c4: <reference osisRef="Job.26.5-Job.7.5">Job 26:5-7   5</reference>   - The shades are put to pain <div eID="gen7982" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7983" type="x-p"/> Deep under the waters and their inhabitants.   6  Sheôl is naked before him, <div eID="gen7983" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7984" type="x-p"/> And the abyss hath no covering.   7  He stretched the northern sky over the emptiness; <div eID="gen7984" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7985" type="x-p"/> He hung the earth upon nothing. <div eID="gen7985" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7986" type="x-p"/> Bildad has extolled God’s majestic, awe-inspiring rule in the heights of heaven, His immediate surrounding; Job continues the strain, and celebrates the extension of this rule, even to the depths of the lower world. The operation of the majesty of the heavenly Ruler extends even to the realm of shades; the sea with the multitude of its inhabitants forms no barrier between God and the realm of shades; the marrowless, bloodless phantoms or shades below writhe like a woman in travail as often as this majesty is felt by them, as, perhaps, by the raging of the sea or the quaking of the earth. On רפאים, which also occurs in Phoenician inscriptions, vid., <hi type="italic">Psychol</hi>. S. 409; the book of Job corresponds with <reference osisRef="Ps.88.11">Psa 88:11</reference> in the use of this appellation. The <hi type="italic">sing</hi>. is not רפאי (whence רפאים, as the name of a people), but רפא (רפה), which signifies both giants or heroes of colossal stature (from רפה = Arab. <hi type="italic">rafu‛a ,</hi> to be high), and the relaxed (from רפה, to be loose, like Arab. <hi type="italic">rafa'a ,</hi> to soften, to soothe), i.e., those who are bodiless in the state after death (comp. חלּה, <reference osisRef="Isa.14.10">Isa 14:10</reference>, to be weakened, i.e., placed in the condition of a <hi type="italic">rapha</hi>). It is a question whether יחוללוּ be <hi type="italic">Pilel</hi> (Ges.) or <hi type="italic">Pulal</hi> (Olsh.); the <hi type="italic">Pul.,</hi> indeed, signifies elsewhere to be brought forth with writing (<reference osisRef="Job.15.7">Job 15:7</reference>); it can, however, just as well signify to be put in pain. On account of the reference implied in it to a higher causation here at the commencement of the speech, the <hi type="italic">Pul</hi>. is more appropriate than the <hi type="italic">Pil.;</hi> and the pausal <hi type="italic">â</hi>, which is often found elsewhere with <hi type="italic">Hithpael</hi> (<hi type="italic">Hithpal</hi>.), <reference osisRef="Ps.88.14">Psa 88:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.33.5">Job 33:5</reference>, but never with <hi type="italic">Piel</hi> (<hi type="italic">Pil</hi>.), proves that the form is intended to be regarded as passive.
entries.5b468916d4cf16618fc6fab04996ede7b3cc6571: <reference osisRef="Job.26.8-Job.10.8">Job 26:8-10   8</reference>  He bindeth up the waters in His clouds, <div eID="gen7987" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7988" type="x-p"/> Without the clouds being rent under their burden.   9  He enshroudeth the face of His throne, <div eID="gen7988" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7989" type="x-p"/> Spreading His clouds upon it. 10  He compasseth the face of the waters with bounds, <div eID="gen7989" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7990" type="x-p"/> To the boundary between light and darkness. <div eID="gen7990" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7991" type="x-p"/> The clouds consist of masses of water rolled together, which, if they were suddenly set free, would deluge the ground; but the omnipotence of God holds the waters together in the hollow of the clouds (צרר, <hi type="italic">Milel</hi>, according to a recognised law, although it is also found in Codd. accented as <hi type="italic">Milra</hi>, but contrary to the Masora), so that they do not burst asunder under the burden of the waters (תּחתּם); by which nothing more nor less is meant, than that the physical and meteorological laws of rain are of God’s appointment. <reference osisRef="Job.26.9">Job 26:9</reference> describes the dark and thickly-clouded sky that showers down the rain in the appointed rainy season. אחז signifies to take hold of, in architecture to hold together by means of beams, or to fasten together (vid., Thenius on 1Ki 6:10, comp. <reference osisRef="2Chr.9.18">2Ch 9:18</reference>, מאחזים, <hi type="italic">coagmentata</hi>), then also, as usually in Chald. and Syr., to shut (by means of cross-bars, <reference osisRef="Neh.7.3">Neh 7:3</reference>), here to shut off by surrounding with clouds: He shuts off פּני־כסּה, the front of God’s throne, which is turned towards the earth, so that it is hidden by storm-clouds as by a סכּה, <reference osisRef="Job.36.29">Job 36:29</reference>; Psa 18:12. God’s throne, which is here, as in 1Ki 10:19, written כּסּה instead of כּסּא (comp. Arab. <hi type="italic">cursi</hi>, of the throne of God the Judge, in distinction from Arab. <hi type="italic">'l - ‛arš ,</hi> the throne of God who rules over the world),<note placement="foot">According to the more recent interpretation, under Aristotelian influence, Arab. <hi type="italic">'l - ‛rš</hi> is the outermost sphere, which God as πρῶτον κινοῦν having set in motion, communicates light, heat, life, and motion to the other revolving spheres; for the <hi type="italic">causae mediae</hi> gradually descend from God the Author of being (<hi type="italic">muhejji</hi>) from the highest heaven into the sublunary world.</note> is indeed in other respects invisible, but the cloudless blue of heaven is His reflected splendour (<reference osisRef="Exod.24.10">Exo 24:10</reference>) which is cast over the earth. God veils this His radiance which shines forth towards the earth, פּרשׁז אליו עננו, by spreading over it the clouds which are led forth by Him. פּרשׁו is commonly regarded as a Chaldaism for פּרשׁז (Ges. §56, Olsh. §276), but without any similar instance in favour of this vocalizaton of the 3 <hi type="italic">pr. Piel</hi> (<hi type="italic">Pil</hi>.). Although רענן and שׁאנן, <reference osisRef="Job.15.32">Job 15:32</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.3.18">Job 3:18</reference>, have given up the <hi type="italic">i</hi> of the <hi type="italic">Pil.,</hi> it has been under the influence of the following guttural; and although, moreover, <hi type="italic">i</hi> before <hi type="italic">Resh</hi> sometimes passes into <hi type="italic">a</hi>, e.g., ויּרא, it is more reliable to regard פרשז as <hi type="italic">inf. absol</hi>. (Ew. §141, <hi type="italic">c</hi>): <hi type="italic">expandendo</hi>. Ges. and others regard this פרשז as a mixed form, composed from פרשׁ and פרז; but the verb פרשׁ (with <hi type="italic">Shin</hi>) has not the signification to expand, which is assumed in connection with this derivation; it signifies to separate (also <reference osisRef="Ezek.34.12">Eze 34:12</reference>, vid., Hitzig on that passage), whereas פרשׂ certainly signifies to expand (<reference osisRef="Job.36.29-Job.36.30">Job 36:29-30</reference>); wherefore the reading פּרשׂז (with <hi type="italic">Sin</hi>), which some Codd. give, is preferred by Bär, and in agreement with him by Luzzatto (vid., Bär’s <hi type="italic">Leket zebi,</hi> p. 244), and it seems to underlie the interpretation where פרשז עליו is translated by עליו (פּרשׂ) פרש, He spreadeth over it (e.g., by Aben-Ezra, Kimchi, Ralbag). But the Talmud, <hi type="italic">b. Sabbath,</hi> 88 <hi type="italic">b</hi> (פירש שדי מזיו שכינתו ועננו עליו, the Almighty separated part of the splendour of His Shechina and His cloud, and laid it upon him, i.e., Moses, as the passage is applied in the Haggada), follows the reading פּרשׁז (with <hi type="italic">Shin</hi>), which is to be retained on account of the want of naturalness in the consonantal combination שׂז; but the word is not to be regarded as a mixed formation (although we do not deny the possibility of such forms in themselves, vid., <hi type="italic">supra</hi>, p. 468), but as an intensive form of פרשׂ formed by Prosthesis and an Arabic change of <hi type="italic">Sin</hi> into <hi type="italic">Shin</hi>, like Arab. <hi type="italic">fršḥ , fršd , fršṭ ,</hi> which, being formed from Arab. <hi type="italic">frš</hi> = פּרשׂ (פּרשׂ), to expand, signifies to spread out (the legs). <div eID="gen7991" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7992" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="Job.26.10">Job 26:10</reference> passes from the waters above to the lower waters. תּכלית signifies, as in <reference osisRef="Job.11.7">Job 11:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.28.3">Job 28:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Neh.3.21">Neh 3:21</reference>, the extremity, the extreme boundary; and the connection of תּכלית אור is genitival, as the <hi type="italic">Tarcha</hi> by the first word correctly indicates, whereas אור with <hi type="italic">Munach</hi>, the substitute for <hi type="italic">Rebia mugrasch</hi> In this instance (according to <hi type="italic">Psalter</hi>, ii. 503, §2), is a mistake. God has marked out (חן, lxx ἐγύρωσεν) a law, i.e., here according to the sense: a fixed bound (comp. <reference osisRef="Prov.8.29">Pro 8:29</reference> with <reference osisRef="Ps.104.9">Psa 104:9</reference>), over the surface of the waters (i.e., describing a circle over them which defines their circuit) unto the extreme point of light by darkness, i.e., where the light is touched by the darkness. Most expositors (Rosenm., Hirz., Hahn, Schlottm., and others) take עד־תכלית adverbially: most accurately, and refer חג to אור as a second object, which is contrary to the usage of the language, and doubtful and unnecessary. Pareau has correctly interpreted: <hi type="italic">ad lucis usque tenebrarumque confinia;</hi> עם in the local sense, not <hi type="italic">aeque ac,</hi> although it might also have this meaning, as e.g., Ecc 2:16. The idea is, that God has appointed a fixed limit to the waters, as far as to the point at which they wash the <hi type="italic">terra firma</hi> of the extreme horizon, and where the boundary line of the realms of light and darkness is; and the basis of the expression, as Bouillier, by reference to Virgil’s <hi type="italic">Georg</hi>. i. 240f., has shown, is the conception of the ancients, that the earth is surrounded by the ocean, on the other side of which the region of darkness begins.
entries.7ff1fcbceb2e12f0465e5abde331021cedf37591: <reference osisRef="Job.26.11-Job.13.11">Job 26:11-13 11</reference>  The pillars of heaven tremble <div eID="gen7992" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7993" type="x-p"/> And are astonished at His threatening. 12  By His power He rouseth up the sea, <div eID="gen7993" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7994" type="x-p"/> And by His understanding He breaketh Rahab in pieces. 13  By His breath the heavens become cheerful; <div eID="gen7994" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7995" type="x-p"/> His hand hath formed the fugitive dragon. <div eID="gen7995" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7996" type="x-p"/> The mountains towering up to the sky, which seem to support the vault of the sky, are called poetically “the pillars of heaven.” ירופפוּ is <hi type="italic">Pulal</hi>, like יחוללוּ, <reference osisRef="Job.26.5">Job 26:5</reference>; the signification of violent and quick motion backwards and forwards is secured to the verb רוּף by the Targ. אתרופף = התפּלּץ, <reference osisRef="Job.9.6">Job 9:6</reference>, and the Talm. רפרף of churned milk, blinding eyes (comp. הרף עין, the twinkling of the eye, and Arab. <hi type="italic">rff , fut. i. o. nictare</hi>), flapping wings (comp. Arab. <hi type="italic">rff</hi> and <hi type="italic">rfrf , movere, motitare alas</hi>), of wavering thinking. גּערה is the divine command which looses or binds the powers of nature; the astonishment of the supports of heaven is, according to the radical signification of תּמהּ (cogn. שׁמם), to be conceived of as a torpidity which follows the divine impulse, without offering any resistance whatever. That רגע, <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.26.12">Job 26:12</reference></hi>, is to be understood transitively, not like <reference osisRef="Job.7.5">Job 7:5</reference>, intransitively, is proved by the dependent (borrowed) passages, <reference osisRef="Isa.51.15">Isa 51:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.31.35">Jer 31:35</reference>, from which it is also evident that רגע cannot with the lxx be translated κατέπαυσεν. The verb combines in itself the opposite significations of starting up, i.e., entering into an excited state, and of being startled, from which the significations of stilling (<hi type="italic">Niph., Hiph.</hi>), and of standing back or retreat (Arab. <hi type="italic">rj‛</hi>), branch off. The conjecture גּער after the Syriac version (which translates, <hi type="italic">go‛ar bejamo</hi>) is superfluous. רהב, which here also is translated by the lxx τὸ κῆτος, has been discussed already on Job 9:13. It is not meant of the turbulence of the sea, to which מחץ is not appropriate, but of a sea monster, which, like the crocodile and the dragon, are become an emblem of Pharaoh and his power, as Isa 51:9. has applied this primary passage: the writer of the book of Job purposely abstains from such references to the history of Israel. Without doubt, רהב denotes a demoniacal monster, like the demons that shall be destroyed at the end of the world, one of which is called by the Persians <hi type="italic">akomano</hi>, evil thought, another <hi type="italic">taromaiti</hi>, pride. This view is supported by <reference osisRef="Job.26.13">Job 26:13</reference>, where one is not at liberty to determine the meaning by <reference osisRef="Isa.51.9">Isa 51:9</reference>, and to understand נחשׁ בּרח, like תּנּין in that passage, of Egypt. But this dependent passage is an important indication for the correct rendering of חללה. One thing is certain at the outset, that שׁפרה is not <hi type="italic">perf. Piel</hi> = שׁפרה, and for this reason, that the <hi type="italic">Dagesh</hi> which characterizes <hi type="italic">Piel</hi> cannot be omitted from any of the six <hi type="italic">mutae;</hi> the translation of Jerome, <hi type="italic">spiritus ejus ornavit coelos,</hi> and all similar ones, are therefore false. But it is possible to translate: “by His spirit (creative spirit) the heavens are beauty, His hand has <hi type="italic">formed</hi> the flying dragon.” Thus, in the signification to bring forth (as <reference osisRef="Prov.25.23">Pro 25:23</reference>; Pro 8:24.), חללה is rendered by Rosenm., Arnh., Vaih., Welte, Renan, and others, of whom Vaih. and Renan, however, do not understand <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.26.13">Job 26:13</reference></hi> of the creation of the heavens, but of their illumination. By this rendering <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.26.13">Job 26:13</reference></hi> and <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.26.13">Job 26:13</reference></hi> are severed, as being without connection; in general, however, the course of thought in the description does not favour the reference of the whole of half of <reference osisRef="Job.26.13">Job 26:13</reference> to the creation. Accordingly, חללה is not to be taken as <hi type="italic">Pilel</hi> from חול (ליל), but after <reference osisRef="Isa.57.9">Isa 57:9</reference>, as <hi type="italic">Poel</hi> from חלל, according to which the idea of <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.26.13">Job 26:13</reference></hi> is determined, since both lines of the verse are most closely connected. (בּריח) נחשׁ בּרח is, to wit, the constellation of the Dragon,<note placement="foot">Ralbag, without any ground for it, understands it of the milky way (העגול החלבי), which, according to Rapoport, Pref. to Slonimski’s <hi type="italic">Toledoth ha-schamajim</hi> (1838), was already known to the Talmud <hi type="italic">b. Berachoth</hi>, 58 <hi type="italic">b</hi>, under the name of נהר דנוד.</note> one of the most straggling constellations, which winds itself between the Greater and Lesser Bears almost half through the polar circle. <div eID="gen7996" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7997" type="x-p"/> “<hi type="italic">Maximus hic plexu sinuoso elabitur Anguis Circum perque duas in morem fluminis Arctos</hi>.” (Virgil, Georg. i. 244f.) <div eID="gen7997" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7998" type="x-p"/> Aratus in Cicero, <hi type="italic">de nat. Deorum,</hi> ii. 42, describes it more graphically, both in general, and in regard to the many stars of different magnitudes which form its body from head to tail. Among the Arabs it is called <hi type="italic">el - hajje ,</hi> the serpent, e.g., in Firuzabâdi: the <hi type="italic">hajje</hi> is a constellation between the Lesser Bear (<hi type="italic">farqadân</hi>, the two calves) and the Greater Bear (<hi type="italic">benât en - na‛sch ,</hi> the daughters of the bier), “or <hi type="italic">et - tanı̂n ,</hi> the dragon, e.g., in one of the authors quoted by Hyde on Ulugh Beigh’s <hi type="italic">Tables of the Stars,</hi> p. 18: the tanîn lies round about the north pole in the form of a long serpent, with many bends and windings.” Thus far the testimony of the old expositors is found in Rosenmüller. The Hebrew name תּלי (the quiver) is perhaps to be distinguished from טלי and דּלי, the Zodiac constellations Aries and Aquarius.<note placement="foot">Vid., <hi type="italic">Wissenschaft, Kunst, Judenthum</hi> (1838), S. 220f.</note> <div eID="gen7998" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7999" type="x-p"/> It is questionable how בּרח is to be understood. The lxx translates δράκοντα ἀποστάτην in this passage, which is certainly incorrect, since בריח beside נחשׁ may naturally be assumed to be an attributive word referring to the motion or form of the serpent. Accordingly, <reference osisRef="Isa.27.1">Isa 27:1</reference>, ὄφιν φείγοντα is more correct, where the Syr. version is חויא חרמנא, the fierce serpent, which is devoid of support in the language; in the passage before us the Syr. also has חויא דערק, the fleeing serpent, but this translation does not satisfy the more neuter signification of the adjective. Aquila in Isaiah translates ὄφιν μόχλον, as Jerome translates the same passage <hi type="italic">serpentem vectem</hi> (whereas he translates <hi type="italic">coluber tortuosus</hi> in our passage), as though it were בּריח; Symm. is better, and without doubt a substantially similar thought, ὄφιν συγκλείοντα, the serpent that joins by a bolt, which agrees with the traditional Jewish explanation, for the dragon in Aben-Ezra and Kimchi (in <hi type="italic">Lex.</hi>) - after the example of the learned Babylonian teacher of astronomy, Mar-Samuel (died 257), who says of himself that the paths of the heavens are as familiar to him as the places of Nehardea<note placement="foot">Vid., Grätz, <hi type="italic">Geschichte der Juden,</hi> iv. 324. On <reference osisRef="Isa.27.1">Isa 27:1</reference> Kimchi interprets the מבריח differently: he scares (pushes away).</note>  - is called נחשׁ עקלתון, because it is as though it were wounded, and בריח, because it forms a bar (מבריח) from one end of the sky to the other; or as Sabbatai Donolo (about 94), the Italian astronomer,<note placement="foot">Vid., extracts from his המזלות ספר in Joseph Kara’s <hi type="italic">Comm. on Job,</hi> contributed by S. D. Luzzatto in <hi type="italic">Kerem Chemed,</hi> 7th year, S. 57ff.</note> expresses it: “When God created the two lights (the sun and moon) and the five stars (planets) and the twelve מזלור (the constellations of the Zodiac), He also created the תלי (dragon), to unite these heavenly bodies as by a weaver’s beam (מנור אורגים), and made it stretch itself on the firmament from one end to another as a bar (כבריח), like a wounded serpent furnished with the head and tail.” By this explanation בּריח is either taken directly as בּריח, <hi type="italic">vectis</hi>, in which signification it does not, however, occur elsewhere, or the signification <hi type="italic">transversus</hi> (<hi type="italic">transversarius</hi>) is assigned to the בּריח (= <hi type="italic">barrı̂ah</hi>) with an unchangeable <hi type="italic">Kametz</hi>, - a signification which it might have, for brch Arab. <hi type="italic">brḥ</hi> signifies properly to go through, to go slanting across, of which the meanings to unite slanting and to slip away are only variations. בּריח, notwithstanding, has in the language, so far as it is preserved to us, everywhere the signification <hi type="italic">fugitivus</hi>, and we will also keep to this: the dragon in the heavens is so called, as having the appearance of fleeing and hastening away. But in what sense is it said of God, that He pierces or slays it? In <reference osisRef="Isa.51.9">Isa 51:9</reference>, where the תנין is the emblem of Egypt (Pharaoh), and <reference osisRef="Isa.27.1">Isa 27:1</reference>, where נחשׁ בריח is the emblem of Assyria, the empire of the Tigris, the idea of destruction by the sword of Jehovah is clear. The present passage is to be explained according to <reference osisRef="Job.3.8">Job 3:8</reference>, where לויתן is only another name for נחש בריח (comp. <reference osisRef="Isa.27.1">Isa 27:1</reference>). It is the dragon in the heavens which produces the eclipse of the sun, by winding itself round about the sun; and God must continually wound it anew, and thus weaken it, if the sun is to be set free again. That it is God who disperses the clouds of heaven by the breath of His spirit, the representative of which in the elements is the wind, so that the azure becomes visible again; and that it is He who causes the darkening of the sun to cease, so that the earth can again rejoice in the full brightness of that great light, - these two contemplations of the almighty working of God in nature are so expressed by the poet, that he clothes the second in the mythological garb of the popular conception. <div eID="gen7999" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8000" type="x-p"/> In the closing words which now follow, Job concludes his illustrative description: it must indeed, notwithstanding, come infinitely short of the reality.
entries.8d2613204e6504a0dc254c87fb76a9ad44ccce69: <reference osisRef="Job.26.14">Job 26:14</reference> <reference osisRef="Job.26.14">14</reference>  Behold, these are the edges of His ways, <div eID="gen8000" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8001" type="x-p"/> And how do we hear only a whisper thereof! <div eID="gen8001" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8002" type="x-p"/> But the thunder of His might - who comprehendeth it? <div eID="gen8002" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8003" type="x-p"/> These (אלּה retrospective, as in <reference osisRef="Job.18.21">Job 18:21</reference>) are only קצות, the extremest end-points or outlines of the ways of God, which Job has depicted; the wondrous fulness of His might, which extends through the whole creation, transcends human comprehension; it is only שׁמץ דּבר therefrom that becomes audible to us men. שׁמץ (שׁמץ) is translated by Symm. here ψιθύρισμα, <reference osisRef="Job.4.12">Job 4:12</reference>, ψιτηυρισμός; the Arab. <hi type="italic">šamiṣa</hi> (to speak very quickly, mutter) confirms this idea of the word; Jerome’s translation, <hi type="italic">vix. parvam stillam sermonis ejus </hi>(comp. <reference osisRef="Job.4.12">Job 4:12</reference>, <hi type="italic">venas</hi>, tropical for parts), is doubly erroneous: the rendering of the שׁמץ has the antithesis of רעם against it, and דּבר is not to be understood here otherwise than in ערות דּבר, <reference osisRef="Deut.23.15">Deu 23:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.24.1">Deu 24:1</reference> : shame of something = something that excites a feeling of shame, a whisper of something = some whisper. The notion “somewhat,” which the old expositors attribute to שׁמץ, lies therefore in דבר. מה is exclamatory in a similar manner as in <reference osisRef="Ps.89.48">Psa 89:48</reference> : how we hear (נשׁמע, not נשׁמע) only some whisper thereof (בּו partitive, as e.g., <reference osisRef="Isa.10.22">Isa 10:22</reference>), i.e., how little therefrom is audible to us, only as the murmur of a word, not loud and distinct, which reaches us! <div eID="gen8003" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8004" type="x-p"/> As in the speech of Bildad the poet makes the opposition of the friends to fade away and cease altogether, as incapable of any further counsel, and hence as conquered, so in Job’s closing speech, which consists of three parts, <reference osisRef="Job.26.1">Job 26:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.27.1">Job 27:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.29.1">Job 29:1</reference>, he shows how Job in every respect, as victor, maintains the field against the friends. The friends have neither been able to loose the knot of Job’s lot of suffering, nor the universal distribution of prosperity and misfortune. Instead of loosing the knot of Job’s lot of suffering, they have cut it, by adding to Job’s heavy affliction the invention of heinous guilt as its ground of explanation; and the knot of the contradictions of human life in general with divine justice they have ignored, in order that they may not be compelled to abandon their dogma, that suffering everywhere necessarily presupposes sin, and sin is everywhere necessarily followed by suffering. Even Job, indeed, is not at present able to solve either one or other of the mysteries; but while the friends’ treatment of these mysteries is untrue, he honours the truth, and keenly perceives that which is mysterious. Then he proves by testimony and an appeal to facts, that the mystery may be acknowledged without therefore being compelled to abandon the fear of God. Job firmly holds to the objective reality and the testimony of his consciousness; in the fear of God he places himself above all those contradictions which are unsolvable by and perplexing to human reason; his faith triumphs over the rationalism of the friends, which is devoid of truth, of justice, and of love. <div eID="gen8004" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8005" type="x-p"/> Job first answers Bildad, Job 26:1. He characterizes his poor reply as what it is: as useless, and not pertinent in regard to the questions before them: it is of no service to him, it does not affect him, and is, moreover, a borrowed weapon. For he also is conscious of and can praise God’s exalted and awe-inspiring majesty. He has already shown this twice, <reference osisRef="Job.9.4-Job.9.10">Job 9:4-10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.12.13-Job.12.25">Job 12:13-25</reference>, and shows here for the third time: its operation is not confined merely to those creatures that immediately surround God in the heavens; it extends, without being restrained by the sea, even down to the lower world; and as it makes the angels above to tremble, so there it sets the shades in consternation. From the lower world, Job’s contemplation rises to the earth, as a body suspended in space without support; to the clouds above, which contain the upper waters without bursting, and veil the divine throne, of which the sapphire blue of heaven is the reflection; and then he speaks of the sea lying between Sheôl and heaven, which is confined within fixed bounds, at the extreme boundaries of which light passes over into darkness; - he celebrates all this as proof of the creative might of God. Then he describes the sovereign power of God in the realm of His creation, how He shakes the pillars of heaven, rouses the sea, breaks the monster in pieces, lights up the heavens by chasing away the clouds and piercing the serpent, and thus setting free the sun. But all these - thus he closes - are only meagre outlines of the divine rule, only a faint whisper, which is heard by us as coming from the far distance. Who has the comprehension necessary to take in and speak exhaustively of all the wonders of His infinite nature, which extends throughout the whole creation? From such a profound recognition and so glorious a description of the exaltation of God, the infinite distance between God and man is most clearly proved. Job has adequately shown that his whole soul is full of that which Bildad is anxious to teach him; a soul that only requires a slight impulse to make it overflow with such praise of God, as is not wanting in an universal perception of God, nor is it full of wicked devices. When therefore Bildad maintains against Job that no man is righteous before such an exalted God, Job ought indeed to take it as a warning against such unbecoming utterances concerning God as those which have escaped him; but the universal sinfulness of man is no ground of explanation for his sufferings, for there is a righteousness which avails before God; and of this, job, the suffering servant of God, has a consciousness that cannot be shaken.  <chapter eID="Job.26"/> <div eID="gen8005" type="x-p"/>

                  <ns0:p n="3">3. How hast thou counselled <ns0:hi>him that hath</ns0:hi> no wisdom <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">Either 1.                   <ns0:p n="4">4. To whom hast thou uttered words <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">For whose Instruction hast thou uttered these things? For mine?
